messages.subject: Spatial line transect models
parts:
I'm in the process of extrapolating density estimates based on model cova=
riates following this basic procedure:
1) do transect-based surveys using relatively short and numerous transect=
s
2) estimate densities in different habitat types
3) extrapolate densities to the transect level by dividing the observed c=
ount of organisms along a transect divided by (2 * Effective Strip Width =
* length of transect)
4) use GLM/GAM modeling to model transect-level density estimates as a fu=
nction of habitat covariates
5) extrapolate model across a geographic area

I have a question relating to steps 3 & 4. Basically, wouldn't one expec=
t zero-inflation in step 3 because you're effectively multiplying an obse=
rved density by a scaling factor, but multiplying an observed density of =
0 times a scaling factor doesn't alter the observed density to account fo=
r detectability. I don't see anything in Advanced Distance sampling (par=
ticularly section 4.3.2) regarding this. If it's already been addressed =
somewhere, I'd love to be pointed in the right direction! I'm using zero=
-inflated modeling to attempt to account for this, and I would like to kn=
ow if my overall conceptualization of the issue is valid (see below for m=
ore details on my conceptualization).=20

Thanks!
Philip Shirk



If my short explanation didn't make sense, here's a more detailed attempt=
to explain it:

In order to estimate detectability, distance-based density estimation use=
s the combined data from all transects. (Individual transects are needed=
only to estimate variation in the estimate.) Conceptually, the observed=
density is always below the true density because one can miss an organis=
m that is actually present, but one cannot see an organism that is not th=
ere (this can be ensured by excluding any uncertain =E2=80=9Csightings=E2=
=80=9D from the analysis). The estimate of detectability is then used as=
a scaling factor to adjust observed densities to account for detectabili=
ty. Similarly, density can be extrapolated down to the individual transe=
ct using the effective transect width as a scaling factor for the observe=
d densities. This is useful when organisms were observed along a transec=
t. However, when no organisms were observed along a transect, multiplyin=
g a scaling factor times zero does not alter the estimate. In the case w=
here no organisms were observed because there were no organisms to observ=
e, the final estimate of zero density is still correct. When no organism=
s are observed because of poor detection, the scaling factor fails to acc=
ount for this because it is being multiplied times zero. As a result, tr=
ansect-level density estimates will be zero-inflated, despite an accurate=
regional density estimate. As we expect excess zeros, zero-inflated mod=
els may be most useful for modeling transect-level density estimates.
